question.en: What is the difference between merging and rebasing, and when would you choose each?

answer.en: A merge combines histories and can create a merge commit, preserving the branch topology. A rebase replays commits on a new base, producing new commit identities and a more linear history. I usually rebase a private feature branch to update it or clean it before review, then merge or fast-forward it according to the team policy. I avoid rebasing a branch others have already based work on, because rewriting its published commits forces them to reconcile divergent histories. The choice is therefore not just aesthetic: merge preserves shared history; rebase is useful when I alone control the commits being rewritten.

question.en: The same textual conflict appears once when you merge a branch, but five times when you rebase it onto the same base. Why?

answer.en: A merge performs a single three-way merge, so you resolve the conflict once and record the resolution in one merge commit. A rebase replays each commit onto the new base individually, so every replayed commit that touches the conflicting hunk can raise the same conflict again, and each resolution is baked into that commit's replayed copy (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase). This is why well-scoped commits, or squashing first, reduce rebase pain: fewer replays means fewer chances to resolve the same hunk.

question.en: main has not moved since you created your feature branch. You merge the branch into main and the log shows no merge commit. Why, and what would --no-ff change?

answer.en: When the current branch is an ancestor of the branch being merged, Git fast-forwards: it moves the branch pointer and creates no merge commit, so the feature commits land directly on main's line. `git merge --no-ff` forbids the fast-forward and forces a merge commit even when none is needed, preserving the shape of the feature branch as a visible group with a single revertable merge point (https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Basic-Branching-and-Merging).

question.en: How do you safely resolve a conflict during a rebase?

answer.en:
First I inspect the conflicted files and the intended result, rather than blindly choosing “ours” or “theirs.” I edit the files to a valid combined version, remove conflict markers, and run focused tests. Then I stage the resolved files with `git add` and run `git rebase --continue`. If the current commit is no longer needed, I can use `git rebase --skip` only after verifying that it is genuinely redundant. If the operation is going in the wrong direction, `git rebase --abort` returns the branch to its pre-rebase state. I never force-push the result without checking the remote and coordinating if the branch is shared.

```bash caption="The core inspect, resolve, continue, or abort sequence."
git status
# edit conflicted files and remove markers
git add path/to/file
git rebase --continue
# or, if the rebase should be abandoned:
git rebase --abort
```

question.en: During `git rebase main` on your feature branch, a conflicted file offers 'ours' and 'theirs'. Which one is your branch's version?

answer.en: Neither merge intuition applies. The git-rebase documentation is explicit: a rebase replays each commit from the working branch on top of the upstream branch, so when a conflict happens the side reported as 'ours' is the so-far rebased series starting with the base (main), and 'theirs' is the working branch; the sides are swapped relative to a merge (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase). Resolving with `git checkout --ours` during a rebase therefore keeps main's side and discards your own change.

question.en: When is `git rebase --skip` the right call, and what does it actually do to your work?

answer.en: Skip drops the commit currently being replayed entirely and continues with the next one. It is correct only when that commit's change is already present in the new base, for example when the same patch was applied upstream, so the replay is a guaranteed no-op that conflicts trivially. Before skipping I verify the change really exists upstream, for instance by diffing the commit against the base; otherwise the commit's change is simply gone from the rebased branch (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase).

question.en: How would you choose between trunk-based development, GitHub Flow, and Gitflow?

answer.en: I would start with release cadence, integration frequency, compliance gates, and whether several production versions must be supported. Trunk-based development keeps one main source of truth and relies on frequent integration, automation, and feature flags. GitHub Flow uses short-lived feature branches that merge to main when ready. Gitflow adds long-lived integration and release branches, which can suit scheduled releases but increases pipeline and merge complexity. The workflow must match the delivery system: branch proliferation should not become a substitute for deployment controls. I would validate the choice with a small pilot and measure lead time, conflict rate, failed changes, and rollback performance.

question.en: Trunk-based development integrates into main constantly. How does half-finished work reach main without users seeing it, and what does that demand from the pipeline?

answer.en: Incomplete changes merge behind feature flags or other inert paths: the code deploys continuously, but the behavior stays off or limited to selected contexts until the flag changes. That demands strong automated tests on every integration, flag hygiene (owner, default-safe state, expiration date), and a fast way to turn the flag off. Without that maturity, trunk-based degrades into either a broken main or a pile of permanent flags (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-cicd-litmus/understanding-cicd.html).

question.en: A team wants release control, so it keeps one long-lived branch per environment (dev, staging, main) and cherry-picks fixes between them. What problems does that create?

answer.en: Cherry-picking copies a change as a new commit identity, so the same logical fix exists several times and the branches drift apart; later merges re-encounter those changes as conflicts or duplicates. Release gating has moved from the deployment system (pipelines, promotions, approvals) into branch topology, which is harder to audit and slower to roll back. The guidance is to keep one main source of truth and put release control in the delivery pipeline rather than in branch proliferation (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/choosing-git-branch-approach/choosing-git-branch-approach.html).
